questions.q: How many physical qubits does the Shor code use to protect 1 logical qubit, and why that number?
options: 9 -- 3 outer phase-flip blocks, each inner-encoded with the 3-qubit bit-flip code (3x3=9)
9 -- simply 9 independent copies of the data qubit
6 -- 3 for bit-flips and 3 for phase-flips, used separately
3 -- the bit-flip and phase-flip codes are applied to the same 3 qubits twice
questions.explain: Concatenating the phase-flip code (3 outer blocks) with the bit-flip code (3 inner qubits per block) gives 3x3=9 total physical qubits, as verified by the construction.

questions.q: In the Shor code, what catches an X error on one of the 9 physical qubits?
options: The inner bit-flip code covering that qubit's block, exactly as in the standalone 3-qubit bit-flip code
The outer phase-flip code, measured across all 9 qubits at once
Nothing -- X errors are not correctable by the Shor code
A separate ancilla qubit not part of the 9-qubit encoding
questions.explain: X errors are handled locally within each 3-qubit inner block by that block's bit-flip code, before they can propagate to the outer code.

questions.q: Why does the Shor code also correct Z errors, unlike the bit-flip code alone?
options: A Z error on any qubit within a block flips that whole block's relative phase the same way, which the outer phase-flip code (operating at the block level) detects and corrects
Z errors are automatically fixed by the inner bit-flip code
The Shor code cannot actually correct Z errors, only X errors
Z errors never occur on 9-qubit encoded states
questions.explain: The outer phase-flip code treats each 3-qubit block as one effective 'qubit' and catches phase disagreements between blocks, which is exactly how a Z error anywhere inside a block gets caught and corrected.

questions.q: Why is a Y error (X and Z on the same physical qubit) also correctable by the Shor code?
options: The X part is caught by the relevant inner bit-flip code and the Z part is caught by the outer phase-flip code, independently and simultaneously
Y errors are impossible on any encoded quantum state
Y errors require a completely separate third layer of encoding not present in the Shor code
The Shor code converts every Y error into a harmless identity operation automatically
questions.explain: Because the inner and outer codes operate on non-interfering information (bit values within a block vs. relative phase across blocks), they independently catch and fix the X and Z components of a Y error.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the Shor code is historically important but not what real fault-tolerant hardware roadmaps use today?
options: Scaling the Shor code to handle more simultaneous errors requires higher concatenation levels, which grows physical-qubit cost exponentially, and it doesn't match real hardware's local connectivity constraints
The Shor code has since been mathematically disproven
The Shor code requires more than 9 qubits in practice, contradicting its own definition
Real hardware roadmaps have abandoned error correction entirely in favor of the Shor code's inner layer only
questions.explain: The Shor code proved QEC was possible, but its exponential scaling cost and qubit-connectivity requirements are why the surface code (chapter 5), not concatenated Shor-style codes, is the leading practical candidate for real hardware.
